doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Playing the Sauter and Gil Evans books
summary: His career alternating between Sauter's and Evans's books, and Evans on composer versus orchestrator.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. We hope they’re alive. Did you bring some other things here you wanted to do?
Yeah, well these are kind of notes that I thought would refresh my memory in case I needed it but I don’t think I do. The one thing I wanted to allude to was the fact that with

Red Norvo I was playing a book by Eddie Sauter. And I left and went with Claude, I was playing a book by Gil Evans. And then after the war I would join Ray McKinley playing Eddie Sauter’s book. Then I left Ray to go back with Claude, like it was going home, an old home, and it was back to Gil Evans. And you know I played those books, I knew it was great but I never really appreciated it. Such giant writers.
Well especially being a writer yourself, you can appreciate the lines and how they used instruments.

Yes. Gil know I used to say I’m not a composer. Well he was you know. But he’d say I’m not a composer, he’d say Eddie’s a composer. He said I’m an orchestrator. He said Eddie could use — he didn’t use this expression precisely — but Eddie could use help with his orchestrating, he thought Eddie could improve upon his colors and combinations and everything. But he said Eddie is a composer, I’m not. So it’s kind of interesting, not necessarily factual, but— that’s about all of it, really.
